title: Assets
author: kalvinbastello
selftext: What do you all use for assets? I have a need for some spritesheets and can't find something that does a decent job. It always gives me extra limbs or merges cells. I ended up having an artist make me a spritesheet for an asset so I could have something to use for a proof of concept, but for a project I'll probably never try to commercialize +100 per asset isnt very sustainable.

comments.body: Itch io and OpenGameArt are usually the go-to for 2D spritesheets in that size range. Quality varies but there are some solid packs if you dig a bit. comments.author: Tyrannicus100BC
comments.body:
Ask your coding agent to build you a generative art pipeline on top of nano banana. It will happily build some offline scripts for you to run that accept input prompts for visual descriptions and then build sprite sheets. Iterate with AI on the pipeline until it’s building your sprite sheets with the right layout and animation. Once the tool is stable, then start mass producing the variety you need. 

With these tool, the real limit is your imagination and bravery to ask for audacious things and then have the patience to iterate on it until it works well.

replies.author: Tyrannicus100BC
replies.body: I just quickly threw this together, but here is an example of a prompt you should feed into your coding agent of choice (OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Google Gemini). This prompt will build you a series of python scripts. You then use the python scripts to generate your characters and their animations. Now here is the interesting part, the first version of this tool might not be great. But let the agent build it, try using it, and then tell the agent what is wrong with the sprite sheets it's generating. Are the character's feet not staying put? Is there too much forward movement in the walk animations? Do the animations not perfectly loop? Just talk to the agent and ask it to iterate on the python scripts by giving it clear instructions about what is wrong with the sprite sheets that it is generating. It might take a few tries, but this will set you up to have a reliable, reusable pipeline for generating all of the art in your game in exactly the style you want. Good luck!

replies.author: Tyrannicus100BC
replies.body:
Technical Prompt for Coding Agent

Role: You are a Senior Tools Engineer specializing in Generative AI pipelines for game development.

Objective: Build a Python-based pipeline that utilizes the Nano Banana model to generate game character concept art and subsequent animated sprite sheets.

Stage 1: Concept Generation (Base Image)

* Functionality: Create a script that takes a descriptive text prompt and generates a high-fidelity base character concept.
* Requirements: \* The output must be a single, clear image.
   * The tool should allow for iterative refinement (running the script multiple times) until a "Base Image" is confirmed by the user.
   * Store the seed and prompt of the confirmed Base Image to maintain style DNA.

Stage 2: Animated Sprite Sheet Generation

* Functionality: Once a Base Image is selected, generate a secondary script to produce a grid-based sprite sheet.
* Input Parameters:
   * Base Image Path: The reference character from Stage 1.
   * Sprite Dimensions: (e.g., 64x64, 128x128).
   * Sheet Dimensions: Total grid size (e.g., 4 columns by 4 rows).
   * Animation Description: A text prompt describing the action (e.g., "walking cycle," "attack swing," "idle breathing").
* Technical Constraints:
   * Character Consistency: Use the Base Image as a strong structural and aesthetic reference to ensure the character doesn't "morph" between frames.
   * Looping Logic: The prompt engineering sent to Nano Banana must emphasize that the last frame must transition smoothly back to the first.
   * Transparency: If possible, include a post-processing step to remove backgrounds or ensure the generation uses a solid, easily removable color (like a chroma key green or magenta).

Deliverables:

1. A modular CLI or simple Web UI (like Streamlit) to handle both stages.
2. An optimized prompt-template system that translates simple user descriptions into high-quality instructions for Nano Banana.
3. Error handling for API timeouts or image generation failures.

replies.author: kalvinbastello
replies.body:
Week later, thought I'd update.

I tweaked the tool more and started producing images. I never got to use the tool for spritesheets because I couldn't even get a good image. I think with **a lot** of patience you could get the right image, but you have to be incredibly specific and know the right keywords to use. Any reference to something that could be on a person (body for example) will try to put a human in the picture. 

I used AI to help me try to get the right terms, and we only ever got half close. I'm not picky at all and I couldn't get close.

Feels like you need to have a good concept of art/styling terms to know what to put in there. At that point you might have the skills to be able to start drawing your own. 

Wont uninstall, but ultimately abandoning for now. I can tell you I have an easy 12-160 hours into just getting this tool up and going without satisfactory results.

YMMV. Hope this helps someone in the future. 

u/Tyrannicus100BC thanks for the thoughtful response though.

comments.author: macuseri686
comments.body:
Using a normal AI model like Nano Banana wont work for spritesheets and pixel art, because AI models cant output transparency, and image models alone have no understanding of animation.

Most pixel-sprite AIs (like Retro Diffusion) are pretty limited. They’re mainly tuned for **bipedal humans** and usually only give you idle/walk cycles, which breaks down fast once you need monsters, turrets, creatures, vehicles, or non-humanoid stuff.

That gap is actually why I built **GameLab Studio** ([https://gamelabstudio.co](https://gamelabstudio.co/?ref=reddit.com)). It’s designed for **game assets, not just characters**, and it’ll generate consistent pixel-art sprites, animations *and* full transparent bg spritesheets for **anything:** creatures, machines, towers, VFX, projectiles, etc. Animations aren’t locked to walk/idle either; you can generate attack, fire, spin, explode, transform, whatever the gameplay needs.

It also enforces consistency across scale, palette, and angles, by using already generated angles of the same asset for reference, so you don’t end up with “AI asset soup” during prototyping.

We also have a seamless tileable edge-aware texture generation model

Looks like auto transparent background on animation misses a few pixels here and there inside the image, but it's better than the chroma key and trying to remove yourself.
